B1.title: Book One: God
B1.bookSummary:
Book One opens the Summa Contra Gentiles with Aquinas's statement of purpose: the office of the wise man is to consider the highest causes of things, and since the ultimate end of the whole universe is the true good understood by the first intellect, that is God, wisdom's proper task is to make God known and to defend that knowledge against error. Aquinas explains that a twofold truth about God is available to us—truths reason can demonstrate, such as God's existence and unity, and truths that exceed reason and must be received by faith, such as the Trinity—and that this book confines itself to what unaided reason can establish, since the Gentiles and philosophers to whom it is addressed do not accept the authority of Scripture. This is why the work proceeds by philosophical demonstration throughout rather than by appeal to revealed authority.

The book's first great task is to prove that God exists, and Aquinas assembles a series of arguments culminating in the same five ways later summarized in the Summa Theologiae: from motion to a first unmoved mover, from the order of efficient causes to a first uncaused cause, from possibility and necessity to a being that exists necessarily of itself, from the graded perfections found in things to a being of maximal perfection, and from the governance of the world to an intelligent orderer. Having secured God's existence, Aquinas turns to the divine nature and proceeds, as he will again in the Summa Theologiae, chiefly by the way of negation: God is shown not to be a body, not composed of matter and form, not identical with any of His accidents, not distinct from His own essence, and not composed of essence and existence—God's very act of being is His essence, so that God alone exists necessarily and simply by virtue of what He is.

From this foundation of absolute simplicity Aquinas derives God's other attributes at length: perfection (God lacks nothing that belongs to the fullness of being), goodness (God is goodness itself, the good toward which every other good is ordered), infinity, the divine presence in all things by essence, power, and knowledge, immutability, eternity (God's mode of existence is a single, undivided "now" without succession), and unity (there can be only one God, since a plurality of necessary beings sharing one nature is impossible). Substantial treatises follow on God's intellect—that God understands Himself and all things through Himself, without discursive reasoning, and that His understanding is His very substance—and on the divine will, life, beatitude, and love. The book closes by establishing that God acts through intellect and will rather than by natural necessity, that His will is free with respect to creatures even though necessary with respect to Himself, and that in God there is joy, love, and even something rightly called liberality and mercy—concepts drawn from human experience but purified of every imperfection when applied to the God whose existence and nature this book has labored, step by demonstrative step, to establish by reason alone.

B2.title: Book Two: Creation
B2.bookSummary:
Having established in Book One what reason can know of God considered in Himself, Aquinas turns in Book Two to God considered as the principle of all other things—that is, to creation. He opens by explaining why the consideration of creatures belongs to the philosophy of God at all: since God is the first cause of all being, knowledge of creatures as His effects both manifests His power and wisdom and strengthens faith, and error about creation inevitably breeds error about the Creator. Aquinas therefore argues at length that it is proper to God, and to God alone, to create—to bring things into being from absolutely nothing, as opposed to the merely natural production of one thing from pre-existing matter—since only an agent of infinite power can bridge the whole distance between non-being and being. Creation is shown to be a free act flowing from God's will and wisdom rather than a necessary emanation, refuting both the eternity-of-the-world arguments of some philosophers and any suggestion that the created order limits or exhausts divine power.

The book then examines what creatures are in themselves, distinguishing them from God by the fundamental fact that every creature is composed of essence and the act of existing it receives from God, whereas in God alone essence and existence are identical. Every creature is thus radically dependent, receiving and continually needing to receive its being as a participation in God's own subsistent being; yet this dependence does not diminish creaturely reality, goodness, or genuine causal power—Aquinas insists that creatures are true secondary causes, not mere occasions for divine action. A long central section addresses the necessity of diversity among creatures: why there must be a graded multiplicity of kinds of being rather than a single created type, so that the whole created order together, rather than any single creature, reflects the fullness of the divine goodness.

Aquinas devotes substantial treatment to the angels as purely spiritual, incorporeal substances—their manner of knowing, their will, their number, and their hierarchical distinction from one another by degrees of intellectual perfection rather than by matter. He then turns to the corporeal creation and, at greatest length, to man as the creature that stands at the junction of the spiritual and material orders. The human soul is defended as the substantial form of the body, one in essence though possessing vegetative, sensitive, and intellectual powers; Aquinas refutes rival theories that would make the soul a mere harmony of bodily qualities or reduce the intellect to a single separate substance shared by all human beings, insisting instead that each person possesses an individual intellectual soul capable of knowing the natures of all things.

The book closes by examining the will as an appetite that necessarily seeks the good in general but is free with respect to particular goods, and by defending human free choice against determinism, showing at length how God's foreknowledge and providential ordering of all things—even future contingent acts—is entirely compatible with, and indeed the very ground of, genuine human freedom, since God causes not only that things exist but the manner of their existing, including the contingent and free manner proper to rational creatures.

B3.title: Book Three: Providence and Divine Governance
B3.bookSummary:
Book Three is the longest book of the Summa Contra Gentiles and turns from what God is and what God creates to how God governs what He has made. Aquinas opens by establishing that every agent acts for an end, that God Himself is the last end of all things, and that all creatures, each according to its own mode, are ordered toward God as their good—non-rational creatures by natural inclination, rational creatures uniquely through knowledge and love. This sets up the book's two great movements: an extended treatise on divine providence and government, and, arising directly out of it, a treatise on the moral life by which rational creatures attain their end.

The providence section argues that God must govern the universe He has created, since a wise cause does not merely produce effects but directs them to their proper ends; Aquinas defends this against objections drawn from the presence of evil, contingency, and chance in the world, showing that particular providence extends even to individual creatures and events without either destroying secondary causality or being frustrated by it. He examines how intellectual creatures are governed differently from others—through law, merit, and reward rather than by natural necessity alone—and how divine providence permits evil for the sake of a greater good without being its cause.

Aquinas then asks directly in what human happiness consists, methodically excluding wealth, honors, fame, power, bodily goods, pleasure, the moral virtues themselves, and even the philosophical contemplation of separate substances, arguing instead that man's ultimate felicity can be found only in the contemplative knowledge of God—a perfect knowledge unattainable by natural powers in this life and reserved for the vision of the divine essence in the next. From this account of the end flows the book's treatment of the means: the cardinal virtues of prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance are examined as the stable dispositions by which reason governs action and passion, and the theological virtues of faith, hope, and charity as the supernatural dispositions, given by grace, that orient a person directly toward God as last end.

A major treatise on law follows, distinguishing the eternal law by which God orders the whole universe from the natural law—the rational creature's own participation in that eternal law, known through the basic inclinations and precepts accessible to every human reason—and explaining how positive human and divine laws derive their binding force from this natural foundation. The book also treats sin and vice at length as disordered turnings away from man's true end, examines the different kinds and gravity of sin, and closes with an extended treatise on grace: since man's true end exceeds what nature alone can attain, Aquinas argues that grace is strictly necessary to heal, elevate, and direct the human will toward God, and considers how grace relates to merit, predestination, and the mystery of some being freed from sin while others are not.

B4.title: Book Four: Salvation and Christ
B4.bookSummary:
Books One through Three of the Summa Contra Gentiles deliberately confined themselves to what natural reason can establish about God, creation, and providence; Book Four turns to truths that exceed reason entirely and can be known only because God has revealed them. Aquinas explains at the outset why such truths, though undemonstrable by philosophy, are not thereby irrational: reason can still show that they are not impossible, defend them against objections, and find fitting arguments (rationes convenientiae) for why God should have arranged things as He did, even where reason alone could never have discovered the truths in the first place.

The book opens with the Trinity, examining the divine processions of the Word and the Holy Spirit and the distinction of Persons within the one divine essence—material Aquinas had reserved from Book One precisely because it belongs to revealed rather than demonstrable theology. From the Trinity the book moves to the Incarnation, arguing at length for its fittingness: that it was supremely appropriate for the divine Word to unite Himself to human nature in one Person while remaining fully God and becoming fully man, so as to restore a fallen humanity from within. Aquinas defends the orthodox account of the hypostatic union against the ancient Christological errors—Arianism, Nestorianism, Eutychianism, and others—showing how Christ possesses two complete and distinct natures, divine and human, united in a single divine Person, with a true human body, a true rational human soul, and a true created human will alongside His divine will.

A substantial treatise follows on the sacraments as the means by which the grace won by Christ's Incarnation, passion, and death is communicated to the faithful across time. Aquinas explains the fittingness of God using visible, created signs to confer invisible grace, given human nature's dependence on the senses, and examines each sacrament in turn—Baptism as the necessary gateway that incorporates a person into Christ and remits sin, Confirmation, the Eucharist (treated with particular care as the sacrament in which Christ's own body and blood are truly present and offered, perpetuating His one sacrifice and nourishing the Church), Penance, and the remaining sacraments of healing and vocation, examining their matter, form, minister, and effects.

The book closes by turning from the beginning of the world to its end: the resurrection of the body, the last judgment, the eternal punishment of the damned and the eternal beatitude of the blessed, and the final state of the whole created order. In this way Book Four completes the movement of the entire Summa Contra Gentiles—from God as first principle known by reason in Book One, through creation and providence in Books Two and Three, to God as the last end of all things, attained through Christ, in Book Four—showing that natural reason and revealed faith, far from competing, together trace the single arc from creation back to the Creator.
